reference.source: DeLee, Drez & Miller's Orthopaedic Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: Presents with deep posterior hip, buttock or groin pain that may radiate distally, characteristically worsened by hip extension, adduction and external rotation.
Pain is typically reproduced during the terminal stance phase of a long stride; the long-stride walking test provokes symptoms whereas short strides relieve them.
Oedema, and in chronic cases fatty infiltration, of the quadratus femoris muscle on MRI is the hallmark imaging finding.
Narrowing of both the ischiofemoral space (between lateral ischium and lesser trochanter) and the quadratus femoris space supports the diagnosis.
It is more common in women, related to a wider pelvis, coxa valga and increased femoral anteversion.
Secondary causes include hip instability, proximal femoral or ischial malunion, prior arthroplasty and space-occupying lesions.

First-line management is activity modification, physiotherapy to correct pelvic mechanics, and an image-guided local anaesthetic and corticosteroid injection into the quadratus femoris, which is also diagnostic.
Refractory cases may be treated by lesser trochanter resection or endoscopic decompression, addressing any underlying morphology or instability.
reference.pathophysiology: The ischiofemoral space is bounded by the lateral cortex of the ischial tuberosity and the medial and posterior aspect of the lesser trochanter, and transmits the quadratus femoris muscle. Congenital or acquired narrowing of this corridor causes dynamic entrapment of quadratus femoris, particularly during hip extension combined with adduction and external rotation, when the space narrows further. Contributing factors include coxa valga, an increased femoral neck-shaft angle or anteversion, prominence of the ischium or lesser trochanter, hip instability, and post-traumatic or post-surgical malalignment. Repeated impingement produces muscle oedema, tears and eventually fatty atrophy, and may irritate the adjacent hamstring origin and sciatic nerve.
additionalDifferentials: Deep gluteal syndrome with sciatic nerve entrapment
Femoral neck or ischial stress fracture
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the pelvis with measurement of the ischiofemoral and quadratus femoris spaces
MRI assessment of quadratus femoris oedema, tears or fatty atrophy
Dynamic ultrasound of the ischiofemoral interval
Image-guided diagnostic local anaesthetic injection into the quadratus femoris
Radiographs to assess coxa valga and proximal femoral morphology
Assessment of femoral version by CT or MRI
redFlags: Progressive sciatic neurological deficit, indicating significant nerve involvement
Rest pain or night pain suggesting a neoplasm around the ischium or proximal femur
A palpable soft-tissue mass narrowing the space
Bilateral symptoms with systemic features prompting a search for an underlying disease
reference.prognosis: Many patients improve with conservative measures and image-guided injection, particularly when a reversible mechanical driver is present. Surgical decompression or lesser trochanter resection gives good reported outcomes in carefully selected refractory cases.
pitfalls: Interpreting a narrowed ischiofemoral space in isolation as diagnostic, since space narrowing occurs in asymptomatic individuals and must be correlated with quadratus femoris signal change and clinical findings.
Relying on neutral-position static MRI, which can miss impingement that only occurs dynamically in extension and adduction.
Mislabelling the condition as piriformis syndrome or a simple hamstring strain.
Ignoring associated femoral version or instability, leading to persistent symptoms after isolated soft-tissue treatment.
references: DeLee, Drez & Miller's Orthopaedic Sports Medicine
management: Activity modification avoiding provocative hip extension, adduction and external rotation, adopting a shorter stride to unload the ischiofemoral space
Physiotherapy targeting hip and core strengthening, gait retraining and stretching of the quadratus femoris and hip external rotators
Simple analgesia and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for pain arising from quadratus femoris oedema
Image-guided local anaesthetic and corticosteroid injection into the quadratus femoris for diagnostic confirmation and symptom relief
Address underlying mechanical drivers such as coxa valga, increased femoral anteversion or hip instability
Refer to orthopaedic surgery for arthroscopic decompression or lesser trochanter resection in refractory cases
